clue.text: Imagined state of Iowa supporting university better than others

indicators.note: in a down clue a supporting piece sits underneath, so the state abbreviation goes after the rest

blocks.note: U is the standard abbreviation for university
to top others is to beat them
IA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Iowa

explanation.surface: Some booster claims Iowa is a dream state that props up a university outshining all others.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'supporting' puts Iowa's letters at the bottom, beneath the university and the word for beating others.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is Thomas More's invented perfect commonwealth, so it is literally an imagined state.

clue.text: Benefit of Japanese drink?

blocks.note: first meaning: advantage
second meaning: Japanese rice wine

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'Benefit of Japanese drink' is not a health claim but two separate meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: One does something for someone's sake, meaning for their good; and the same spelling names the rice wine served warm in Japan.

clue.text: Colloidal suspension worried US oilmen

indicators.note: worried in the sense of fretted at or pulled about, so these letters are disturbed into a new order

blocks.note: taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: American oil workers are anxious about some chemistry involving droplets suspended in liquid.
explanation.definitionFit: An emulsion is a mixture of fine droplets of one liquid dispersed in another, a kind of colloid.

clue.text: Halfwit adult speaks emptily

indicators.note: emptily means with the inside removed, leaving just the outside letters of the word

blocks.note: A is the film classification for adult
only the first and last letters of speaks remain

explanation.surface: A grown-up fool talks without saying anything of substance.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone an ass is calling them a fool, so it is a synonym for a halfwit.

clue.text: Regularly annoys doctor regarding query of one whose stomach keeps rumbling?

definitions.text: query of one whose stomach keeps rumbling?

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so take every other letter starting from the first

blocks.note: the first, third and fifth letters of annoys
MO is a Medical Officer
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Someone keeps pestering a doctor about a patient with a noisy, grumbling stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a whole little scene: a hungry person, stomach still rumbling, asks 'Any more?' at the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A still-hungry diner asks whether there is any more food, so the two words are exactly that question.

clue.text: Condition of country – almost unserviceable

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: a state is a nation or country
US is a crossword abbreviation for unserviceable, i.e. useless

explanation.surface: A report says a nation's infrastructure is nearly beyond repair.
explanation.walkthrough: US standing for unserviceable is a familiar crossword shorthand, as in 'it's no US'.
explanation.definitionFit: Status means standing or state of affairs, so it is a synonym for condition.

clue.text: Air letter page occasionally run over given very small weight

indicators.note: occasionally means now and again, so only every other letter is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters of page
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a run
O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over
a gramme is a tiny unit of mass

explanation.surface: Instructions for preparing a lightweight letter: a page, run over, weighed carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: R and O come from cricket scoring, where run and over are abbreviated in scorebooks.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerogramme is a thin prepaid sheet that folds into its own envelope for sending by airmail.

clue.text: Full of vigour, mum spread cake covering

indicators.note: something full of a thing holds it inside, so one piece surrounds another here

blocks.note: a familiar word for mother
as dye or ink spreads, it ran
zip means energy or liveliness

explanation.surface: An energetic mother busily spreads icing over a cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a present-tense instruction but is past tense, the way colours spread in the wash; the vigour sits inside the second piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Marzipan is the almond paste rolled over fruit cakes beneath the icing.

clue.text: Sham opponent inexperienced bloke on street is boxing

indicators.note: on here means placed next to, so the street abbreviation simply joins up with the other pieces

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
raw means green or untrained
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: A novice fighter on the street spars with a pretend adversary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is boxing' adds only the picture: a straw man is the dummy opponent one knocks down easily; the letters come entirely from street, inexperienced and bloke.
explanation.definitionFit: A straw man is a weak invented position or adversary set up only so it can be easily knocked down.

clue.text: Palm on the other hand read oddly, on reflection

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so only first and third letters remain
a reflection in a mirror is back to front, so the kept letters run the other way

blocks.note: then can mean 'but on the other hand', as in 'but then again'
the first and third letters of read

explanation.surface: A palmist reads a hand strangely, then has second thoughts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm on the other hand' looks like palmistry, but the hand is a phrase meaning 'then again'.
explanation.definitionFit: The thenar is the fleshy ball of the palm at the base of the thumb, an anatomical term for that part of the palm.

clue.text: Simple diet trashed – fine results if it's ignored

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked and scattered, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A dieter abandons their plain regime and is pleased with the results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fine' is a penalty, not 'good'; ignoring this road rule leads to a ticket.
explanation.definitionFit: Exceeding the maximum legal speed on a road earns a monetary penalty, which is the fine described.

clue.text: Seepage of unopened alcohol

indicators.note: unopened means without its opening, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: booze is informal for alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Liquor leaks from a bottle that has never been opened.
explanation.definitionFit: Ooze is a slow trickle of liquid escaping, which is what seepage means.

clue.text: Expedition in South American distant island

blocks.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south
A is a standard abbreviation for American
far means a long way off
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: An explorer's journey to a remote South American island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American' reads as one place but supplies two separate abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: A safari is an organised trip or expedition, especially to view wildlife in Africa.

clue.text: Legal conveyance once brief lawsuit is over

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the last letter of the word goes
turned over means flipped, so in this down entry the letters read upwards

blocks.note: a case is a lawsuit brought before a court

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned property transfer was settled once a short court action ended.
explanation.walkthrough: In old English law, sac was a lord's right to hold a court, granted along with land; 'once' marks it as historical.
explanation.definitionFit: Sac was a jurisdiction granted, i.e. conveyed, with a manor in Anglo-Saxon law, now obsolete.

clue.text: A broad smile about the French now and then being sailors

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped round another
now and then means at intervals, so alternate letters are kept

blocks.note: taken as written
a beam is a wide grin
les is French for 'the' before a plural
the second and fourth letters of being

explanation.surface: A grin spreads over French faces now and then as sailors arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The broad smile goes round the French article; 'being' is fodder for the alternate letters, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Able seamen are trained ratings in the Royal Navy or merchant navy, i.e. sailors.

clue.text: Decree right to restrict prices being adjusted

indicators.note: adjusted means altered, so these letters are rearranged
restricting something hems it in, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: RT is an abbreviation for right
taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A government acts to hold down prices that have been altered.
explanation.walkthrough: The two-letter abbreviation for right splits to hold the rearranged prices.
explanation.definitionFit: A rescript is an official edict or ruling, such as a papal or imperial reply with the force of law.

clue.text: Reportedly securing spot for a fan, say

indicators.note: reportedly means as told by others, so we want a word that sounds like the one the clue points to

blocks.note: sealing means securing, fastening shut

explanation.surface: Someone is said to have found a place to install a cooling fan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' suggests a supporter needing a seat; it is the electric fan, often mounted overhead.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceiling fans hang from the overhead surface of a room, so it is a place where a fan can be fixed; 'say' marks an example.

clue.text: One honourably discharged rues time at sea

indicators.note: at sea means confused and adrift, so these letters are muddled up

blocks.note: taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A sailor discharged with honour regrets the years spent on board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discharged' suggests the navy, but it means retired from office.
explanation.definitionFit: An emeritus professor has retired honourably, keeping their title as a mark of distinction.

clue.text: Anthers and filaments sustained energy

blocks.note: first meaning: plural of a flower's male organ, each made of anther and filament
second meaning: endurance

explanation.walkthrough: The botanical plural of stamen is rarely seen, so the second meaning is the everyday one.
explanation.definitionFit: A stamen consists of an anther on a filament, and one plural is stamina; endurance is the familiar sense.

clue.text: Burlesque effort incorporating a piece of underwear

indicators.note: incorporating means taking into its body, so one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: a try is an attempt
a vest is an undershirt in British usage

explanation.surface: A comic stage act includes someone stripping to their underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: A vest in Britain is the garment worn under a shirt, not a waistcoat.
explanation.definitionFit: A travesty is a grotesque mockery or parody, which is what a burlesque is.

clue.text: Outstanding location – not Poland!

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letters are taken out

blocks.note: a place is a location
PL is the international code for Poland

explanation.surface: Someone praises a superb spot, insisting it is anywhere but Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: Ace as an adjective is informal for excellent or first-rate.

clue.text: So far sailor is circumnavigating eye of rough storm

indicators.note: the eye of a storm is its centre, so only the middle letter is used
sailing all the way round something encloses it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: 'as far' and 'so far' are interchangeable in comparisons, so so stands for as
an old salt is a seasoned sailor
the central letter of rough

explanation.surface: So far a sailor has circled round the eye of a violent tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storm' is the verb, as troops storm a fort; the sailor goes round the middle of rough.
explanation.definitionFit: To storm a position is to attack it violently, which is to assault it.

clue.text: Pressure causes these journalists to probe nuisances

indicators.note: something that probes goes inside, so one piece is put into the other

blocks.note: bores are tiresome people or things
eds are editors

explanation.surface: Pressure leads reporters to investigate tiresome people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure' reads as stress on journalists, but it is physical pressure on the skin of someone confined to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedsores are ulcers caused by prolonged pressure on the skin from lying in one position.

clue.text: Fret in aisle, purchasing eye liner

indicators.note: purchasing means acquiring and holding, so the run of letters is held within these words

blocks.note: the letters run across the boundaries of these words

explanation.surface: A shopper worries in a supermarket aisle while buying makeup for the eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eye liner' is cosmetics in the surface, but here it is what lines the inside of the eye.
explanation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eyeball.

clue.text: Repay some scavengers

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the letters are only a portion of the following word

blocks.note: the letters sit inside this word

explanation.surface: Pay back a few of the creatures that feed on leftovers.
explanation.definitionFit: To avenge a wrong is to repay it with retaliation.

clue.text: Worn down foundation

blocks.note: first meaning: past participle of grind, reduced by friction
second meaning: a basis

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the verb grind in its past participle; the second is the noun for a base.
explanation.definitionFit: Ground is what has been ground, i.e. abraded; it is also the basis on which something rests.

clue.text: Bread fibre

blocks.note: first meaning: a flat Middle Eastern bread, a variant spelling of pitta
second meaning: a strong plant fibre from agave leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'fibre' suggests dietary roughage in bread, but it is a separate plant material.
explanation.definitionFit: Pita is both a flat pocket bread and the tough fibre obtained from agave and related plants.

clue.text: GMB possibly on air? Tuned out

indicators.note: out means disordered or wrong, so these letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken letter by letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Is Good Morning Britain being broadcast? The listener has switched off.
explanation.walkthrough: GMB looks like the breakfast TV show Good Morning Britain, but it is also a large British general trade union; 'possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The GMB is one of Britain's largest unions of workers, so it is an example of an organised labour body.

clue.text: Finds fault with horses

blocks.note: first meaning: criticises persistently
second meaning: old or poor-quality horses

explanation.walkthrough: 'Finds fault with horses' sounds like a picky judge at a show; split it into two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To nag is to carp at someone; a nag is also a worn-out horse, here in the plural.

clue.text: Without hesitation, adolescent produces dish

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: a teen is a teenager
ur is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A teenager confidently serves up a meal without pausing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without hesitation' reads as 'promptly', but 'without' is the old sense of outside: the adolescent goes round the hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: A tureen is a deep lidded serving dish for soup.

clue.text: Man of action fired extremely insulting worker

indicators.note: extremely refers to the extremes, so the first and last letters are kept

blocks.note: lit means set alight
the first and last letters of insulting
a worker ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: A dynamic man sacks an extremely rude employee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of action' suggests a doer, but an action here is a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: A litigant is a party to a legal action, so a person involved in an action at law.

clue.text: Official proceedings mostly produce an effect

indicators.note: mostly means not entirely, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: acts are formal records of proceedings, as in the Acts of Parliament

explanation.surface: Formal meetings largely achieve results.
explanation.definitionFit: A medicine that acts takes effect, so to act is to produce a result.
